question: Palma City Council’s protection of a Francoist monument linked to the crime that was the La Desbandá massacre

The Spanish Government has added the monument of Sa Feixina (in Palma de Mallorca) to the state register of symbols contrary to democratic memory. The monument was erected during the Franco dictatorship to honour those ‘fallen for God and for Spain’, including crew members of the cruiser Baleares, which was involved in mass killings of civilians during the Spanish civil war, including the La Desbandá massacre.

Simultaneously, Palma City Council granted the monument the highest degree of heritage protection, announcing legal action to prevent it from being removed. Those events reflect the fact that democratic memory policies are being questioned. This contrasts with both the European Union’s commitment to victims and the values set out in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union.
It also runs counter to the European Parliament resolution of 25 October 2018 on the rise of neo-fascist violence in Europe, which emphasises combating the glorification of dictatorships. 1.
Does the Commission consider the institutional protection of symbols exalting dictatorships to be compatible with EU values and the abovementioned resolution?
Does the Commission intend to address such situations in its rule of law reports or through other mechanisms for monitoring respect for the values of Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.7.2026) It is the responsibility of the Member States and regional and local authorities to deal with the classified monuments. It is not for the Commission to interpret national rules concerning such matters or to issue warnings or directions in connection with those rules.

In general, the Commission, within its competences, has always been strongly committed to ensuring the respect of the victims and the memory of the crimes committed by totalitarian regimes. The Commission supports Member States in the area of remembrance through targeted financial support in programmes like the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) Programme1.

CERV supports activities on the causes of totalitarian regimes and the commemoration of their victims under the Remembrance call for proposals, aiming at facilitating the reconciliation process by encouraging discussion, sharing of experiences and promoting best practices. The Commission is fully committed to using all tools at its disposal to uphold the values under Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union.

Through the annual Rule of Law Report, the Commission monitors developments related to the rule of law in all Member States, covering four pillars: justice systems, anti-corruption frameworks, media pluralism and freedom and other issues related to checks and balances. Issues linked to victims of totalitarian regimes do not fall within the Report’s scope.
